overview.title: Residual projections in code (Listings 9.2-9.3) and a residual_block function
overview.main_topic: Keras code for residual connections around blocks that change the number of filters (end of Listing 9.2) or downsample with max pooling (Listing 9.3), and the beginning of a small ConvNet built from a reusable residual_block utility function.
overview.central_idea: When a block changes the channel count, project the residual with Conv2D(filters, 1); when it also max-pools by 2, use Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2). Use padding='same' inside the block. Packaging this logic in a residual_block(x, filters, pooling) function lets you build a whole ConvNet from repeated residual blocks.
overview.importance: Turns the shape-matching rules of p.297 into working code, and the residual_block helper embodies the MHR idea of reuse (p.294) together with residual connections; the same structure scales up into the mini Xception model (p.305).
learning_objectives: Read Listing 9.2 and explain why the residual needs a Conv2D(64, 1) projection.
Read Listing 9.3 and explain why the projection uses strides=2.
Trace tensor shapes through both listings.
Explain the role of padding='same' in both the convolution and the max pooling layer.
Understand the structure and arguments of the residual_block utility function.

summary:
**End of Listing 9.2 (target block changing the number of filters).** After `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))` (p.297): a `Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")` produces `x`, which is set aside as `residual`. The block is a single `Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")`: it increases the filters from 32 to 64 and uses same padding to avoid downsampling. Because the residual only had 32 filters, `layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual)` projects it to the correct shape, and `layers.add([x, residual])` merges them.

**Listing 9.3 (target block including a max pooling layer).** Same start, but the block is `Conv2D(64, 3, ..., padding="same")` followed by `MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")`. Both layers use same padding so that the only downsampling is the 2x pooling. The residual projection is `Conv2D(64, 1, strides=2)`: `strides=2` matches the downsampling of the pooling layer. Then the block output and residual have the same shape and are added.

**A simple residual ConvNet.** To make it concrete, the book builds a ConvNet from blocks of two convolution layers and an optional max pooling layer, each wrapped in a residual connection. It starts with `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))` and `Rescaling(1.0 / 255)`, then defines a utility function `residual_block(x, filters, pooling=False)`: save the residual, apply two `Conv2D(filters, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")` layers, and, if `pooling`, apply `MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")` and project the residual with a strided `Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2)`. The `elif` branch, the add, the three block calls and the classifier head are on p.299.

paragraphs.excerpt: To make these ideas more concrete, here’s an example of a simple ConvNet structured
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces an example ConvNet structured into a series of blocks, each made of two convolution layers and one optional max pooling layer, with a residual connection around each block.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of writing the residual logic inline for each block, the code defines it once in a function and calls it several times with different filter counts: modularity and reuse in code, mirroring the Xception block structure of Figure 9.2.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the template for building deep residual ConvNets in Keras, and it shows how the MHR principle (p.294) translates into a few lines of Python.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the function returns a tensor, so blocks compose like layers: x = residual_block(x, 32, pooling=True) and so on. This is a common idiom for functional-API models.

terminology.meaning: A Python function that adds a group of layers to the graph; here residual_block.
The pooling flag decides whether a block downsamples.

connections: p.294: models built from repeated blocks.
p.299: the rest of the function and the model summary.
p.305: the mini Xception model uses the same structure with separable convolutions and batch normalization.

concepts.name: Residual connection
concepts.definition: Adding a block's input (possibly projected) back to its output.
concepts.intuition: A shortcut that preserves the input's information.
concepts.technical: layers.add([x, residual]) after projecting residual with a 1x1 Conv2D when filters change, with strides=2 when the block max-pools by 2.
concepts.misconception: The projection is only needed when shapes differ; otherwise the identity shortcut is used.

concepts.name: 1 x 1 convolution projection
concepts.definition: Conv2D with kernel size 1, used to change the residual's channel count, and with strides to change its spatial size.
concepts.intuition: Re-encode each pixel's channels into the new number of channels; skip every other pixel when strided.
concepts.technical: Conv2D(64, 1) maps 32 to 64 channels (32*64 + 64 = 2,112 parameters); strides=2 halves height and width.
concepts.significance: Makes residual addition possible across shape-changing blocks.
concepts.misconception: A strided 1x1 conv does not average the skipped pixels; it simply samples every second position.

concepts.name: Reusable convolutional block
concepts.definition: A group of layers defined once, here as residual_block, and applied several times.
concepts.technical: Two Conv2D(filters, 3, relu, same) + optional MaxPooling2D(2, same) + residual projection + add.
concepts.significance: Implements the modularity and reuse of the MHR formula.
concepts.misconception: Reusing the block definition does not share weights between blocks; each call creates new layers.

concepts.name: padding='same'
concepts.definition: Padding mode that keeps height and width unchanged for stride-1 convolutions (and gives ceil(n/2) for 2x2 pooling).
concepts.intuition: Add a border of zeros so the window can be centred on edge pixels.
concepts.technical: Without it, a 3x3 conv shrinks each spatial dimension by 2 and pooling on odd sizes drops the last row/column.
concepts.significance: Lets the residual projection match the block output with just a channel change and a stride.
concepts.misconception: It does not prevent downsampling by strides or pooling; it only avoids downsampling due to padding.

math.title: Shape bookkeeping for Listing 9.3
math.source_text: Not printed as a formula; derived from Listing 9.3 (callout: 'We use strides=2 in the residual projection to match the downsampling created by the max pooling layer').

variables.meaning: Height, width and channels of a tensor (batch axis omitted).

math.operations: Top row: the block path. Bottom row: the residual projection. Both end at the same shape, so they can be added.
math.purpose: Shows why strides=2 and 64 filters are the right projection settings.
math.interpretation: Channels are matched by the filter count; spatial size is matched by the stride.
math.intuition: Both paths must arrive at the same 'address' before they can be summed.
math.numerical_example: Input 32 x 32 x 3 -> Conv2D(32, 3) valid: 30 x 30 x 32. With strided 1x1 conv: output size $\lfloor (30-1)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 15$.

code.title: The target block changing the number of output filters (continued from p.297)
code.original_code:
x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")(inputs)
residual = x
x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
residual = layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual)
x = layers.add([x, residual])
code.what_it_does: Builds a residual connection around a convolution that increases the filters from 32 to 64, projecting the residual with a 1x1 Conv2D so the shapes match. (Imports and inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3)) are on p.297.)

line_explanations.explanation: First convolution: 32 filters, 3x3, valid padding, giving (None, 30, 30, 32).
The layer around which the residual connection is created: it increases the number of output filters from 32 to 64; padding='same' avoids downsampling due to padding. Output (None, 30, 30, 64).
The residual only had 32 filters, so a 1 x 1 Conv2D projects it to the correct shape, (None, 30, 30, 64).
Now the block output and the residual have the same shape and can be added.

code.algorithm: Save residual -> transform -> project residual -> add.
code.theory_link: Implements the 'linear projection of the residual' rule from p.297.

parameters.name: Conv2D(64, 1)
parameters.role: 1x1 projection from 32 to 64 channels, no activation.

parameters.name: padding="same"
parameters.role: Keeps 30 x 30 so only the channel count differs.

pitfalls: Omitting the projection raises a shape-mismatch error in layers.add (32 vs 64 channels).
Dropping padding='same' would make the block output 28 x 28, which a 1x1 conv without strides cannot match.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written check (not from the book)
import keras
from keras import layers
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))
x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")(inputs)
residual = x
x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
residual = layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual)
print(x.shape, residual.shape)  # (None, 30, 30, 64) (None, 30, 30, 64)

code.title: The target block including a max pooling layer
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))
x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")(inputs)
residual = x
x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")(x)
residual = layers.Conv2D(64, 1, strides=2)(residual)
x = layers.add([x, residual])
code.what_it_does: Residual connection around a two-layer block (conv + 2x2 max pooling) that changes both the channel count and the spatial size; the residual is projected with a strided 1x1 convolution.

line_explanations.explanation: The block of two layers around which the residual connection is created: Conv2D(64, same) gives (None, 30, 30, 64), MaxPooling2D(2, same) gives (None, 15, 15, 64). padding='same' in both layers avoids downsampling due to padding.
strides=2 in the residual projection matches the downsampling created by the max pooling layer: (None, 15, 15, 64).
Now the block output and the residual have the same shape and can be added.

code.algorithm: Save residual -> conv + pool -> strided 1x1 projection of residual -> add.
code.theory_link: Implements 'use strides in the residual projection to match any downsampling caused by a max pooling layer' (p.297). Same pattern as the 'Conv 1x1, stride=2x2' shortcuts in Figure 9.2.

parameters.name: MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")
parameters.role: Halves height and width (ceil for odd sizes).

parameters.name: Conv2D(64, 1, strides=2)
parameters.role: Projects 32 -> 64 channels and halves height and width.

pitfalls: Forgetting strides=2 leaves the residual at 30 x 30 vs 15 x 15.
With an odd spatial size and pooling without same padding, the shapes would differ by one (e.g. floor vs ceil).

code.title: A simple ConvNet with residual blocks (beginning; continues on p.299)
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))
x = layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255)(inputs)

def residual_block(x, filters, pooling=False):
    residual = x
    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(filters, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    if pooling:
        x = layers.MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")(x)
        residual = layers.Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2)(residual)
code.what_it_does: Defines the model input with pixel rescaling and the first part of a utility function that applies a convolutional block with a residual connection and optional max pooling. The elif branch (projection without pooling when channels change), the add, the return, the three block calls and the classifier are on p.299.

line_explanations.explanation: 32 x 32 RGB input; Rescaling(1.0 / 255) maps pixel values from [0, 255] to [0, 1].
Utility function to apply a convolutional block with a residual connection, with an option to add max pooling.
Save the block input as the residual.
Two 3x3 convolutions with `filters` channels, ReLU, same padding (no spatial change).
If we use max pooling, we add a strided convolution to project the residual to the expected shape: pooling halves the size, Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2) matches it.

code.inputs_outputs: residual_block takes a tensor x and returns (after the code on p.299) a tensor with `filters` channels, halved in size if pooling=True.
code.algorithm: Block = two same-padded convs (+ optional pool), residual projected as needed, then added.
code.theory_link: Combines the patterns of Listings 9.2 and 9.3 into one reusable function: modularity and reuse (p.294) plus residual connections (p.297).

parameters.name: filters
parameters.role: Number of filters of both convolutions and of the projection.

parameters.name: pooling
parameters.role: Whether the block ends with 2x2 max pooling (and a strided projection).

pitfalls: The function is incomplete on this page; it needs the elif/add/return lines on p.299 to work.
Each call creates new layers; the blocks do not share weights.

deeper.title: Why same padding matters for residual matching
deeper.body: Beyond the book: take Listing 9.3 without same padding. Conv2D(64, 3) valid would give 28 x 28; MaxPooling2D(2) valid gives 14 x 14. A strided 1x1 projection of the 30 x 30 residual gives 15 x 15, so the add fails (14 vs 15). With same padding the block gives 30 -> 30 -> 15, matching the projection's 15. That is exactly the book's reason: 'to avoid downsampling due to padding.'

deeper.title: Identity vs. projection shortcuts
deeper.body:
Three cases appear across pp.297-299:

| block changes | shortcut |
|---|---|
| nothing | identity: `residual = x` |
| channels only | `Conv2D(filters, 1)` (Listing 9.2; `elif` branch on p.299) |
| channels and size (pooling) | `Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2)` (Listing 9.3; `if pooling` branch) |

The identity shortcut is free and purest; projections add a few parameters and are used only when needed.

misconceptions.claim: In Listing 9.3 the max pooling is applied to the residual as well.
misconceptions.correction: The residual is downsampled by the strided 1x1 convolution, not by pooling.
It projects only when pooling is used or (p.299) when the number of channels changes; otherwise the shortcut is the identity.

misconceptions.claim: Calling residual_block twice with the same filters reuses the same weights.
misconceptions.correction: Each call creates new Conv2D layers with their own weights; only the code is reused.

takeaways: Channel change only: project the residual with Conv2D(filters, 1).
Channel change plus 2x2 max pooling: project with Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2).
Use padding='same' in the block's convolution and pooling layers so only intentional downsampling occurs.
A residual_block(x, filters, pooling) function packages the pattern for reuse across a ConvNet.

questions.question: In Listing 9.2, why is residual = layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual) needed?
questions.answer: The residual has 32 channels but the block output has 64; the 1x1 conv projects the residual to 64 channels so they can be added.
questions.explanation: From the callout: 'The residual only had 32 filters, so we use a 1 x 1 Conv2D to project it to the correct shape.'

questions.question: Why does Listing 9.3 use strides=2 in the residual projection?
options: To match the downsampling created by the max pooling layer
To reduce the number of parameters
questions.answer: To match the downsampling created by the max pooling layer
questions.explanation: The callout says so explicitly. The projection has no activation, its parameter count does not depend on strides, and padding is handled by padding='same' in the block.

questions.question: Give the output shapes of the block path and the residual path in Listing 9.3 just before layers.add.
questions.explanation: Input 32x32x3 -> Conv2D(32,3) valid: 30x30x32 (residual). Block: Conv2D(64, same) 30x30x64 -> MaxPool(2, same) 15x15x64. Residual: Conv2D(64,1,strides=2) -> 15x15x64.

questions.question: Why do both the Conv2D and the MaxPooling2D layers in Listing 9.3 use padding='same'?
questions.answer: To avoid downsampling due to padding, so the only change in spatial size is the intentional factor of 2 from pooling, which the strided projection can match exactly.
questions.explanation: Stated in the callout above Listing 9.3; without same padding the sizes would not line up.

questions.question: What does the pooling argument of residual_block control?
options: Whether the block ends with 2x2 max pooling and a strided residual projection
Whether a residual connection is used at all
questions.answer: Whether the block ends with 2x2 max pooling and a strided residual projection
questions.explanation: Inside `if pooling:` the code adds MaxPooling2D(2, padding='same') and Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2) on the residual. ReLU is always used, the residual is always added, and filters is a separate argument.

questions.question: What does Rescaling(1.0 / 255) do at the start of the example model?
questions.answer: It scales pixel values from the 0-255 range to 0-1 before the convolutions.
questions.explanation: Same preprocessing as the chapter 8 ConvNets.

questions.question: Without running it, predict what error would occur if you deleted the residual projection line from Listing 9.3, and why.
questions.answer: layers.add would raise a shape mismatch: (None, 15, 15, 64) vs (None, 30, 30, 32).
questions.explanation: Tests that you can do shape bookkeeping for residual connections.
